planting.note: Mount on bark or hang unpotted in bright, filtered light with free air movement; this species has no soil-based root system and depends on regular misting or soaking to take up water.

directions: Fine, wiry, silver-green leaves radiate from a small central point and multiply into dense hanging clumps, each rosette eventually producing slim spikes of pale violet-blue flowers with a delicate, sweet fragrance detectable at close range. Native to the Atlantic coastal forests of Brazil, it grows fastest and blooms most freely of the fine-leaved tillandsias, forming show-worthy specimen clumps within a couple of seasons when mounted on cork or driftwood. Soak or mist thoroughly two to three times a week and shake off standing water from the leaf axils afterward, since the tightly packed thread-like foliage holds moisture and is prone to rot if it stays wet too long. Give bright, filtered light rather than direct sun for the best growth and most reliable flowering.

planting.note: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright light with good air movement; this species tolerates more direct sun than soft-leaved tillandsias and needs regular soaking or misting rather than soil watering.

directions: Narrow, gently arching leaves densely coated in silvery trichomes build a compact, symmetrical rosette that stores water and reflects intense highland sun, and mature plants send up a striking spike of bright golden-yellow flowers rising from red-tinged bracts. Native to dry, rocky, high-elevation scrub of Bolivia, Paraguay, Argentina, and Uruguay, it is one of the more sun- and drought-tolerant tillandsias in general cultivation and colors up silvery-white with strong light exposure. Soak or mist two to three times weekly and allow the plant to dry fully and quickly afterward, since its arid native habitat makes it more prone to rot than shade-loving forest species if left damp. Provide strong light and excellent air circulation to encourage the densest trichome coat and the most floriferous bloom spikes.

planting.note: Mount on bark or wire into a hanging cluster in bright, filtered light; this true epiphyte has no functional root system for water uptake and relies on regular misting or soaking.

directions: Slender, silvery-gray leaves curve outward from a small clumping base and, in spring, produce short spikes of tiny golden-yellow flowers carrying what many growers consider the most pleasant fragrance of any tillandsia. It ranges across a broad swath of southern South America — Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Paraguay, and Uruguay — growing on trees and rock outcrops from lowland scrub to cooler upland sites, which gives it somewhat better cold tolerance than typical rainforest air plants. Soak or mist two to three times a week, letting the plant dry within a few hours each time, and mount it where the fragrant blooms can be appreciated up close. Clumps multiply steadily from basal offsets into dense, floriferous mounds over a few growing seasons.

planting.note: Mount on bark or driftwood in bright, filtered light with good airflow; this epiphyte has no soil-based roots and needs routine misting or soaking to take up water.

directions: Fine, needle-thin leaves pack tightly into small, dense rosettes that clump readily into low mounds, and mature growths send up short spikes of rose-pink bracts holding deep violet-blue flowers. One of the most widely distributed tillandsias, it is found from Mexico through the Caribbean and across much of South America, and cultivated stock shows considerable variation in leaf color and size depending on the collection locale, from grassy green to nearly black forms. Soak or mist two to three times weekly and let the plant dry within an hour or two, since its fine leaves and tight growth habit hold water at the base if air circulation is poor. Give bright, filtered light to keep the clump compact and to encourage reliable, repeated flowering from each rosette before it eventually offsets and fades.

planting.note: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright light with strong air movement; this desert-adapted species tolerates more direct sun than most tillandsias and needs soaking or misting rather than soil watering.

directions: Silvery-green leaves curl and recurve outward from the center of the rosette in a starburst pattern, and a tall, branching red bloom spike rises well above the foliage at maturity, giving the species its common name. Native to the arid scrub and coastal desert of Baja California and mainland Mexico, it is one of the more sun-tolerant and drought-resistant tillandsias in general cultivation, coping well with strong light and infrequent watering once established. Soak weekly and mist between soakings if grown in a dry indoor environment, always allowing the curled leaf base to dry fully to avoid rot. Its architectural, twisting form and long-lasting red inflorescence make it a favorite mounted specimen plant.
sources: Air Plant Greenhouse nursery culture notes

planting.note: Mount on bark or grow unpotted in bright light with excellent drainage of moisture off the foliage; this desert species is easily overwatered and needs soaking or misting rather than soil culture.

directions: Stiff, narrow, gray-green leaves form a spreading, somewhat succulent rosette, topped by a compact spike of striking wine-purple flowers with a scent many growers describe as cinnamon-like. Endemic to the coastal deserts and dry Andean foothills of Peru, it naturally roots into sand and rock in one of the driest habitats of any cultivated tillandsia, making excess moisture and low light its two biggest cultivation risks. Soak lightly every seven to ten days rather than following a heavier rainforest-species schedule, and always give it the brightest light available, since insufficient sun leads to soft, stretched growth and poor flowering. Its unusual flower color and fragrance make it a standout among species grown primarily for foliage.
sources: Travaldo's Blog — Tillandsia purpurea care and culture

planting.note: Mount securely on heavy bark or grow in a large shallow pot for stability; this is one of the largest cultivated tillandsias and, despite its bulk, still has no soil-based root system for water uptake, so it depends on regular soaking.

directions: The largest species commonly grown in the genus, its thick, frosted gray-green leaves build an enormous rosette that can reach two to three feet across and several pounds in weight, eventually sending up a branched flower spike that towers several feet above the foliage. Native to cliffs and rocky slopes of the Ecuadorian Andes at moderate elevation, it tolerates cooler nights than many lowland tillandsias and, because of its size, is often grown potted or mounted on heavy timber rather than hung loose. Soak weekly, allowing extra time for the dense, overlapping leaf base to dry out fully afterward, since a plant this large holds moisture much longer than small species. The vivipara form is especially prized in cultivation for producing large numbers of pups directly on the spent bloom spike.
sources: Vintage Green Farms — Tillandsia secunda notes

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot of well-draining bromeliad mix or mount epiphytically in bright, filtered shade; keep the central cup topped with water and flush it every couple of weeks.

directions: A cross of Neoregelia carolinae and 'Painted Lady' bred by well-known hybridizer Chester Skotak, 'Morado' forms a tight, symmetrical rosette with a crisp white margin along each leaf that frames waves of pink, rose, and burgundy color developing across the foliage as the plant matures and approaches bloom. The compact, 14 to 16 inch habit and reliably patterned color have made it a popular collector cultivar among named Neoregelia hybrids. Grow in bright, filtered light — stronger light intensifies the leaf coloring, while deep shade keeps the rosette mostly green — and keep the central water-holding cup filled and periodically flushed to prevent stagnation. Propagate by removing and potting rooted offsets once they reach a few inches across.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Neoregelia culture notes

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot of well-draining bromeliad mix or mount epiphytically in bright, filtered shade; keep the central cup filled with water and flush it regularly to prevent stagnation.

directions: Broad, glossy, lime to grass-green leaves form a large, spreading rosette whose tips flush a vivid magenta-pink, an effect that deepens across the whole leaf as flowering approaches, growing to roughly two feet tall and over two feet wide at maturity. As with other tank bromeliads, small flowers form low in the central water-holding cup rather than on a showy spike, so the appeal of 'Passion' lies almost entirely in the bold two-tone foliage contrast. Bright, filtered light produces the strongest magenta color at the leaf tips, while too much shade keeps the plant mostly green and too much direct sun can scorch the broad leaf surface. Keep the central cup topped with fresh water, and divide and pot rooted offsets once established clumps become crowded.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Neoregelia culture notes
Florida Council of Bromeliad Societies — Neoregelia photo index

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant, shaded container specimen, or zone 9b-11 outdoor shade planting in well-draining bromeliad mix; keep the central cup filled with water and refresh it every one to two weeks.

directions: This long-cultivated variegated sport of Neoregelia carolinae carries a bold, lengthwise cream-to-white stripe running down the center of each stiff, glossy, spine-tipped leaf, bordered by clean green margins, in a broad, flat, cartwheel-shaped rosette. As with the species, the innermost leaves flush a brilliant red in the weeks before the small flowers open in the central water cup, giving a striking three-color combination of green, cream, and red that persists for months and gives the cultivar its name. Bright indirect light produces the crispest variegation and the deepest blush color, while low light causes the cream stripe to fade toward pale green; avoid direct sun, which scorches the pale portions of the leaf. Keep the tank filled with water, flush it periodically, and remove rooted offsets to propagate, since variegated offsets do not come reliably true from seed.
sources: Bromeliads.info — Neoregelia carolinae Tricolor growing specifications
